name: Retaining wall

summary: number of wall blocks (Materials needed) is what the Retaining wall calculator works out, and it gets there from the height and the length. That makes it useful for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Retaining wall calculator work?
sections.html:
The Retaining wall calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports number of wall blocks (Materials needed) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (will there be a cap row?); then you type in the height (Wall dimensions), the length (Wall dimensions), the height (Block dimensions) and the length (Block dimensions).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Retaining wall calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Number of wall blocks=rounded up, (height ÷ height) × rounded up, (length ÷ length)
Number of cap blocks=rounded up, (length ÷ length)
Number of wall blocks=rounded up, (height ÷ height) × rounded up, ((-length + length) ÷ length)
Total cost of blocks=single wall block price × rounded up, (height ÷ height) × rounded up, (length ÷ length)
Single cap block price=total cost of cap blocks ÷ rounded up, (length ÷ length)
Single wall block price=total cost of wall blocks ÷ (rounded up, (height ÷ height) × rounded up, ((-length + length) ÷ length))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Retaining wall calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the height and the length — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Retaining wall calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns number of wall blocks (Materials needed), derived from the height and the length. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Retaining wall calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the height and the length, which is 12 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter height (Wall dimensions) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Height (Wall dimensions) opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Retaining wall calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
